cards.source_title: AAIF: Dex Horthy: Long-Running Coding Agents Still Degrade Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.claim: The right abstraction for serious production coding is verifiers around bounded steps, not an open-ended agent loop with permission to keep going.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as his conclusion, backed by SlopCodeBench and the failed HumanLayer factory; the article says he made the open-loop case in Aug 2025 and still holds it.
cards.landing: Phase routine design: bounded phases with explicit verifier gates rather than self-paced loops; reinforces one-phase-per-chat

cards.source_title: AAIF: Dex Horthy: Long-Running Coding Agents Still Degrade Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.claim: Current verification tooling catches functional failures but rarely taste (design/maintainability) failures, which he treats as the root cause of slop.
cards.evidence_detail: Asserted in the talk preview; supported indirectly by SlopCodeBench defect accumulation.
cards.landing: Refuter/reviewer rubric: add explicit maintainability and pattern-precedent checks beyond tests and CI

cards.source_title: AAIF: Dex Horthy: Long-Running Coding Agents Still Degrade Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: one poor decision becomes precedent and then architecture
cards.claim: Agents imitate existing repository patterns, so a single poor early decision is copied and hardens into architecture.
cards.evidence_detail: Paraphrase in the promo article; no number given.
cards.landing: Review step: flag any new pattern a PR introduces; CLAUDE.md 'respect slice boundaries' section

cards.source_title: AAIF: Dex Horthy: Long-Running Coding Agents Still Degrade Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: AI can generate changes in minutes, but humans may need hours
cards.claim: Generation is fast but human comprehension takes hours, so the human understanding step is the bottleneck and the process should be designed around it.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as a constraint teams should accept; no measurement.
cards.landing: One-page owner view and six-question closing message: optimise for owner comprehension cost per PR

cards.source_title: AAIF: Dex Horthy: Long-Running Coding Agents Still Degrade Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Fable and Sol each recorded 10 strict passes
cards.claim: On a SlopCodeBench subset of 6 challenges and 30 checkpoints, Fable and Sol each had 10 strict passes (33.3%) and Kimi K3 runs had 8 and 7; every model accumulated defects as checkpoints continued.
cards.evidence_detail: 6 challenges, 30 checkpoints; Dex admits provider differences are within error bars and not statistically conclusive.
cards.landing: Calibrates trust in agent self-extension over many phases; supports verifiers between phases
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 — SlopCodeBench: Sol, Fable and Kimi

cards.source_title: AAIF: Dex Horthy: Long-Running Coding Agents Still Degrade Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a complex state machine with four Unix processes
cards.claim: HumanLayer's lightly supervised factory ran three to four months, grew to 30,000-40,000 lines with a tangled state machine, and was archived.
cards.evidence_detail: Own failed experiment; line count and duration given, no quality metric.
cards.landing: Rationale for human review at phase boundaries; 3-6 month degradation horizon relevant to a 40-phase plan

cards.source_title: AAIF: Dex Horthy: Long-Running Coding Agents Still Degrade Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: updated roughly 30% each time it's given
cards.claim: The AGNTCon talk is a roughly 159-slide deck that he revises about 30% each time he gives it, so earlier recordings go stale.
cards.evidence_detail: Article statement about talk logistics.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious; useful for dating which version of his claims to trust

cards.source_title: Dev Interrupted: Why software factories fail without humans
cards.author: Dex
cards.claim: Humans must keep understanding what happens in the codebase; thinking cannot be handed to the agent.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated in a panel; summary of auto-transcript.
cards.landing: Owner view and reviewer step: keep a human-readable account of what changed and why

cards.source_title: Dev Interrupted: Why software factories fail without humans
cards.author: Dex
cards.claim: A PR needing under 5% rework indicates good quality, and complaints of too many PRs usually mean too many bad PRs.
cards.evidence_detail: Rule-of-thumb threshold, no data source.
cards.landing: Measure rework per PR (review-driven changes) as a harness health metric; ties to skipped measurement pipeline

cards.source_title: Dev Interrupted: Why software factories fail without humans
cards.author: Dex
cards.claim: Three SF CTOs set tight auto-merge gates (no touching certain code, under ~200 lines, passing checks) and PR counts rose because engineers changed behaviour to qualify.
cards.evidence_detail: Second-hand account of three CTOs with 100+ person teams; 200 lines given as an example.
cards.landing: PR size cap and no-touch zones as mechanical gate in CI or pre-merge check

cards.source_title: Dev Interrupted: Why software factories fail without humans
cards.author: Dex+others
cards.claim: Split a codebase into a 'core' with a high quality bar and a 'pragmatic' zone with a lower bar, forbidden from importing each other; shared code moves into core.
cards.evidence_detail: Attributed to a sandbox-platform founder and principal engineers; Dex endorses it.
cards.landing: Import-linter contracts: tier slices by risk (money, lifecycle, outbox as core) and apply stricter review only there

cards.source_title: Dev Interrupted: Why software factories fail without humans
cards.author: Dex+others
cards.claim: Factory AI banned useEffect in its codebase because agents struggle with React's render model; ban constructs agents handle badly.
cards.evidence_detail: One company example, relayed by Dex.
cards.landing: ESLint no-restricted-syntax rules for constructs agents misuse in the web manager; CLAUDE.md rule converted to lint

cards.source_title: Dev Interrupted: Why software factories fail without humans
cards.author: Dex
cards.claim: 'Night vision' observability and the /showme skill (diffs distilled into snippets, diagrams, summaries) keep humans able to follow automated work.
cards.evidence_detail: Product/practice description; skill released about two weeks before the episode.
cards.landing: Skill candidate for the owner view / PR visual outline; show-me from humanlayer/skills

cards.source_title: Dev Interrupted: Why software factories fail without humans
cards.author: Dex
cards.claim: Every work item needs a named human owner.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated in panel.
cards.landing: Phase routine: name the owner of each phase and PR in the draft PR body

cards.source_title: Dev Interrupted: Why software factories fail without humans
cards.author: Dex
cards.claim: Measure in order of preference: customer outcomes, features shipped or throughput, then PRs, lines of code, tokens spent; and changes compound so bad code taxes every later change.
cards.evidence_detail: Ranking stated in conversation; The Goal recommended as background.
cards.landing: Measurement pipeline (a skipped lever): choose outcome metrics over activity metrics if ever built

cards.source_title: Dev Interrupted: Why software factories fail without humans
cards.author: Dex
cards.claim: HumanLayer ran a lights-off factory for about four to five months from roughly November, found the result tangled, and rebuilt from scratch on better design principles.
cards.evidence_detail: Duration differs from the AAIF piece (three to four months); transcript wording unclear.
cards.landing: Timeline for risk: unattended runs degrade within months; keep human gates in the 40-phase plan

cards.source_title: code.talks 2026 Hamburg: Why Software Factories Fail
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: They can write code; they can't yet do architecture.
cards.claim: Until models can architect, humans must stay in the loop above the code deciding what gets built, as the steering wheel rather than a bottleneck.
cards.evidence_detail: Talk abstract only; no data.
cards.landing: Keep architecture and slice-boundary decisions as owner-approved items in the plan, not agent-decided

cards.source_title: code.talks 2026 Hamburg: Why Software Factories Fail
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: maintainability, navigability, blast radius, and outcomes over time
cards.claim: Benchmarks should measure maintainability, navigability, blast radius and outcomes over time rather than test-passing.
cards.evidence_detail: Proposal in abstract.
cards.landing: Reviewer checklist dimensions per PR: blast radius and navigability alongside fail-before/pass-after

cards.source_title: BigGo summary of AIEWF 2026 keynote
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Agents really start to struggle after maybe 3 to 6 months.
cards.claim: Codebases degrade under agents after roughly 3 to 6 months even with advanced prompting.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated from own experience; quoted in third-party summary.
cards.landing: Horizon for the 40-phase plan: schedule a human architecture review before month 3

cards.source_title: BigGo summary of AIEWF 2026 keynote
cards.author: Dex
cards.claim: About 30 minutes of upfront planning (product review, architecture, program design, vertical slices) can save hours of review and keeps line-by-line review feasible; model judges raise the floor, not the ceiling.
cards.evidence_detail: No measurement; benchmark durations (15 min vs up to 400 hours) cited as context.
cards.landing: Plan @ sha step; limits the value of model-judge panels as a quality ceiling

cards.source_title: JetBrains blog: What We Heard at AGNTCon Europe (via daily.dev)
cards.author: Dex
cards.claim: At AGNTCon Europe he said unattended-agent code worsens over time, review is the slowest step even with automation, and teams should plan first, keep reading code as it is produced, and add agentic review and regression testing.
cards.evidence_detail: Third-party conference recap, secondhand; original JetBrains page was 403.
cards.landing: Review-as-you-go inside each phase rather than batch review at the end
